proposals.new: Mother must cut short her maternity leave and pay (or Maternity Allowance), taking less than 52 weeks' leave and 39 weeks' pay, for SPL to be available.
proposals.explanation: The sources don't say the mother must be eligible for SMP or Maternity Allowance, so that was replaced with what they do say: she must cut her maternity leave and pay (or Maternity Allowance) short.

claims.claim: To get SPL and ShPP, maternity leave must be cut to less than 52 weeks and maternity pay (or Maternity Allowance) to less than 39 weeks, with the rest used as SPL and ShPP.
claims.quote: To get SPL and ShPP , you or your partner has to: take less than the 52 weeks of maternity or adoption leave and use the rest as SPL take less than the 39 weeks of maternity or adoption pay (or Maternity Allowance) and use the rest as ShPP

claims.claim: The mother must end maternity pay or Maternity Allowance so that she or her partner can get SPL.
claims.quote: The mother or adopter must end any maternity pay, adoption pay or Maternity Allowance so that they or their partner can get SPL .

proposals.old: Child has moved to live primarily with a different parent after separation.
proposals.new: The person who will claim is responsible for the child, for example because they live with the child.
proposals.explanation: Replaced the unsupported condition about the child moving to the other parent after separation with the source's rule on responsibility, which includes living with the child.

claims.claim: You are usually responsible for a child if you live with them or pay towards looking after them.
claims.quote: You’ll usually be responsible for a child if either: you live with them you’re paying at least the same amount as Child Benefit (or the equivalent in kind) towards looking after them

claims.claim: Child Benefit goes to someone responsible for bringing up the child.
claims.quote: You get Child Benefit if you’re responsible for bringing up a child

proposals.old: Parents have separated and current Child Benefit claimant is no longer the main carer.
proposals.new: The current Child Benefit claimant wants someone else to claim Child Benefit for the child.
proposals.explanation: Removed the unsupported 'no longer the main carer' and separation conditions and stated the trigger the source actually gives for changing who gets Child Benefit.

claims.claim: The service applies when the current claimant wants someone else to claim.
claims.quote: Contact the Child Benefit Office if you want someone else to claim Child Benefit, for example, your spouse or partner.

proposals.old: After separation, only one parent can claim Child Benefit per child. If the child's living arrangements change, Child Benefit must be transferred to the main carer.
proposals.new: Only one person can get Child Benefit for a child. If you want someone else to claim, contact the Child Benefit Office, then the other person makes a new claim. If you cannot agree who gets it, HMRC decides.
proposals.explanation: Replaced the unsupported rule that benefit must go to the main carer when living arrangements change with the source's actual process for changing who gets Child Benefit.

claims.claim: Only one person can get Child Benefit for a child.
claims.quote: Only one person can get Child Benefit for a child.

claims.claim: To change who claims, contact the Child Benefit Office and the other person then makes a new claim.
claims.quote: Contact the Child Benefit Office if you want someone else to claim Child Benefit, for example, your spouse or partner. After you’ve done this, tell the other person to make a new claim.

claims.claim: If people responsible for the same child cannot agree, HMRC decides.
claims.quote: If you cannot agree, HM Revenue and Customs ( HMRC ) will decide who will get it.

proposals.old: A statutory service for parents who cannot reach a private maintenance arrangement. CMS calculates payments based on the paying parent's income. A fee applies to use the Collect & Pay service.
proposals.new: A service parents can use instead of a private arrangement to arrange child maintenance. CMS can work out an amount to pay and arrange payments.
proposals.explanation: I removed the word 'statutory', the 'cannot reach' limit, the income basis and the fee/Collect & Pay detail, because the source doesn't state any of them.

claims.claim: Child maintenance can be arranged privately if both parents agree or through the CMS
claims.quote: Child maintenance can be arranged: privately between parents , if both parents agree through the Child Maintenance Service

claims.claim: CMS can work out an amount to pay and arrange payments
claims.quote: The Child Maintenance Service can: work out an amount to pay arrange payments and take action if a parent does not pay

proposals.old: If parents cannot agree privately. CMS calculates based on paying parent's income.
proposals.new: An alternative to arranging child maintenance privately. CMS works out an amount to pay.
proposals.explanation: I removed the claim that CMS is only for parents who cannot agree, and the income basis, because the source supports neither.

claims.claim: CMS is an alternative to a private arrangement
claims.quote: Child maintenance can be arranged: privately between parents , if both parents agree through the Child Maintenance Service

claims.claim: CMS works out an amount to pay
claims.quote: The Child Maintenance Service can: work out an amount to pay

proposals.old: Available to parents who experienced the loss of a baby before 24 weeks gestation (including miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy). Free and optional. The certificate is not a legal document (it cannot be used to claim benefits) and is not added to the GP record. Losses before 1 October 1992 are covered up to 28 weeks. England only; arrives by post within 21 days.
proposals.new: Available to parents who experienced the loss of a baby before 24 weeks of pregnancy. Free and optional. The certificate is not a legal document (it cannot be used to claim benefits) and is not added to the GP record. Losses before 1 October 1992 are covered up to 28 weeks. England only; can take up to 21 days to arrive by post.
proposals.explanation: Removed the unsupported mention of miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy, and changed 'arrives within 21 days' to 'can take up to 21 days', which is how the source puts it.

claims.claim: Available to parents who lost a baby before 24 weeks of pregnancy
claims.quote: you’ve lost a baby before 24 weeks of pregnancy (or 28 weeks before 1 October 1992) you’re one of the baby’s parents or surrogate

claims.claim: Free
claims.quote: It’s free to get a certificate.

claims.claim: Optional
claims.quote: It’s optional.

claims.claim: Not a legal document; cannot be used to claim benefits
claims.quote: The certificate is not a legal document - for example, you cannot use it to claim benefits.

claims.claim: Not added to GP record
claims.quote: The certificate will not be added to your GP record.

claims.claim: Losses before 1 October 1992 covered up to 28 weeks
claims.quote: (or 28 weeks if your pregnancy ended before 1 October 1992)

claims.claim: England only
claims.quote: you live in England

claims.claim: Can take up to 21 days to arrive by post
claims.quote: Your certificate can take up to 21 days to arrive in the post.

proposals.old: For every £8 a parent pays into their account, the government adds £2 (up to £500 per child per quarter, or £1,000 if disabled). Must be in work and earning at least NMW for 16 hours.
proposals.new: For every £8 a parent pays into their account, the government adds £2 (up to £500 per child every 3 months, or £1,000 if the child is disabled). Usually must be in work (or returning to work) and expect to earn at least the National Minimum Wage or Living Wage for 16 hours a week on average. A parent who is not working may still be eligible if their partner works and they get certain benefits.
proposals.explanation: I changed 'must be in work' to 'usually', added the exception for a parent who isn't working but whose partner works, and made the quarterly and disabled-child wording match the source.

claims.claim: For every £8 paid in, the government adds £2.
claims.quote: For every £8 you pay into the account, the government will top it up by £2.

claims.claim: Up to £500 per child every 3 months.
claims.quote: The total top up you can get for each child is £500 every 3 months (up to £2,000 a year).

claims.claim: £1,000 every 3 months if the child is disabled.
claims.quote: This goes up to £1,000 every 3 months if your child is disabled (up to £4,000 a year).

claims.claim: Usually must be working or returning to work.
claims.quote: You’ll usually need to be working (or returning to work)

claims.claim: The earnings threshold is NMW or Living Wage for 16 hours a week on average.
claims.quote: This is the National Minimum Wage or Living Wage for 16 hours a week on average.

claims.claim: A non-working parent may be eligible if the partner works and they get certain benefits.
claims.quote: You may still be eligible if your partner is working and you’re eligible for any of the following:

proposals.old: Mandatory pre-tribunal step for most employment disputes; a free Acas conciliation service that tries to resolve disputes before a tribunal claim is lodged.
proposals.new: Notifying Acas is a required step before most employment tribunal claims (some claims are exempt); Acas then offers voluntary early conciliation, which tries to help resolve the dispute before a tribunal claim.
proposals.explanation: Made it clear that only notifying Acas is required and that taking part in conciliation is voluntary, and dropped 'free', which the sources don't say about early conciliation.

claims.claim: You must notify Acas before making an employment tribunal claim.
claims.quote: You must notify Acas if you want to make a claim to an employment tribunal.

claims.claim: Some claims are exempt from early conciliation.
claims.quote: Some types of claim are 'exempt' from (do not have to go to) early conciliation.

claims.claim: Acas then offers early conciliation.
claims.quote: We will then offer early conciliation.

claims.claim: Early conciliation is voluntary.
claims.quote: Early conciliation is voluntary. You and your employer can choose whether to take part.

claims.claim: It tries to help resolve the dispute before a tribunal claim.
claims.quote: During early conciliation, an Acas conciliator tries to help you reach a legal agreement with your employer. This can help you avoid going to an employment tribunal.
